title: MemTrial: Learning When to Trust Memory in LLM Portfolio Agents
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents for portfolio management learn from experience: they credit each experience in their memory with the outcome of the decisions that used it. In financial markets, however, this outcome mostly reflects the market move shared by all decisions on that date, so the credit tracks the market rather than the experience, and these agents often do worse than simply holding the equal-weight (1/$N$) portfolio. We ask how an agent can credit an experience with what it changes, and answer it by putting memory on trial: drafts of the same decision with and without an experience face the same market, so the outcome they share cancels in their difference. Our agent, MemTrial, drafts each decision with eight combinations of its retrieved experiences, chosen by a fractional factorial design, and credits each experience with its Banzhaf value, the average of these differences. As each date occurs once and each draft is a noisy LLM sample, these credits are noisy and may not hold on new dates. MemTrial therefore pools them across dates and similar experiences with a hierarchical Bayesian model, acts on them only after they have predicted unseen dates, and otherwise stays anchored at a conservative reference such as 1/$N$. On four benchmarks, MemTrial not only benefits from experiences that matter (the best of 15 methods on a semi-synthetic benchmark with known experience quality) but also limits its losses when its values do not hold (at most 2.2\% below 1/$N$ on PortBench and InvestorBench, against 15--38\% for the best experience-learning agent). Averaged over five settings, it improves the utility of the best experience-learning agent by 21.2\%, and with eight LLMs it beats every LLM-based baseline on InvestorBench.
why: LLM portfolio agent memory credit via counterfactual ablation, beats equal-weight framing.

title: Beyond Isolation: LLM-Guided Hypergraph Learning across Documents and Horizons for Volatility Prediction from Conference Calls
abstract: Conference-call-based volatility prediction has mainly followed an isolated information modeling paradigm, treating each transcript as an isolated information source and each forecast horizon as an independent task. This limits comparison with economically comparable peers and the use of risk information shared across horizons. We propose an LLM-Guided Hypergraph Learning framework to address these limitations. We first use LLMs to construct a shared pool of standardized business-condition factors and then build factor-transcript hypergraphs that connect disclosures across firms through shared factors, enabling the model to retrieve comparable historical peer information. The model then explicitly compares focal and peer information and jointly predicts volatility over 5-, 10-, 20-, and 60-day horizons through multi-task learning with horizon-specific modulation. Experiments on 14,896 U.S. earnings conference calls show that the framework consistently outperforms strong transcript-based, graph-based, and financial baselines. Ablation studies confirm the importance of factor-guided peer retrieval, explicit comparison, and cross-horizon learning.
why: LLM-built peer hypergraph for volatility; tests network signal on transcripts.

title: Consistent But Lenient: Large Language Models Versus Human Underwriters on Borderline Consumer Credit Decisions
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are being evaluated, and marketed, as reviewers of consumer credit files, and the case for them rests on a premise: that machine review is more consistent than the human judgment it would replace. This paper tests that premise on matched stimuli. Eight frontier LLMs from three vendors evaluated the same 17 consumer loan files, under the same instructions, as a panel of 61 credit professionals in a prior noise audit, with ten independent runs per model. On clear files, models and humans agree almost perfectly. On the nine borderline files, humans reach Fleiss' kappa of 0.151; the same model across runs reaches 0.854 and different models reach 0.596. Consistency, however, is not calibration. Models approved 79.2% of borderline decisions against 46.3% for humans, ranked the files in nearly the same risk order (Spearman rho = 0.89), and reversed the human majority on three of nine files, including a fouryear-old charge-off that 80% of professionals denied and 95% of model runs approved. Instructing models to adopt 3, 12, or 25 years of experience left approval rates unchanged, whereas human tenure predicts conservatism. LLM review removes the reviewer lottery but replaces sixty-one thresholds with one that no credit committee chose and that differs across vendors by 26 percentage points. Consistency is not a sufficient deployment criterion; threshold calibration is.
why: LLMs versus underwriters on matched files; updates prior on consistency versus calibration.

title: From Financial Scenario Coverage to Economic Decisions with Local Neural and Language Models
abstract: Financial decision support requires a distinction between recognizing plausible price paths, interpreting financial information and choosing economically useful actions. We examine these stages in a local framework combining a compact neural scenario model, B3, with a general-purpose language-model selector, MiDM. The study extends earlier scenario-selection and general decision-model research with a pair-selection objective, financial adaptation and matched execution controls. For S&P 500 scenarios, B3 covers the realized case in its selected pair on 50.81% of 677 five-day-horizon observations and 55.95% of 647 twenty-day-horizon observations, improving on the B2 candidate scorer by 5.91 and 8.66 percentage points. Descriptive paired block-bootstrap intervals exclude zero, but the longer-horizon result remains below the frequency baseline and several rare cases have little or no coverage. In a separate KOSPI experiment, mixed financial training raises MiDM's financial-report and observed-stock comprehension accuracy from 53.91% to 67.19% and from 58.33% to 75.00%, while action-choice accuracy falls from 54.37% to 45.77%. Calibration, stacking and frozen residual architectures do not establish an incremental economic benefit. Simulated MiDM policies earn positive cumulative returns but underperform alwayslong controls using the same support guard. These results identify task-specific improvements and a transfer boundary: broader scenario coverage and better financial comprehension do not establish better investment decisions. All market evaluations reuse previously inspected historical periods; the findings motivate prospective confirmation rather than a claim of deployable alpha.
why: Honest out-of-sample scenario selection with bootstrap; longer horizon underperforms baseline.

title: Who Leads and Who Collects: Algorithmic Collusion in Markets of Heterogeneous Language Models
abstract: Evidence that pricing algorithms collude comes from markets in which every seller runs the same algorithm. We ask what happens when they do not. Four language models from four providers, each at its cheapest tier, price in a four-firm logit Bertrand market without communication, in every homogeneous, two-by-two and fully mixed composition (11 cells, 20 runs, 200 periods). Collusion is a property of the model: Claude and Gemini markets reach 72 to 79 percent of the monopoly rent, DeepSeek markets 24 percent, and GPT markets none, though GPT prices drift above the monopoly level rather than toward competition. Mixing does not reduce collusion by itself. Markets containing Gemini, which opens at the highest price and settles highest, are more collusive than the homogeneous markets they are built from; markets containing Claude, which opens lower and follows its rivals down, are less so; and only the fully mixed market is significantly less collusive than the average homogeneous one. Stability depends on the least stable participant: two GPT firms suffice to keep any market from converging. Inside mixed markets the rent is shared in a transitive order, DeepSeek over Claude over Gemini over GPT, that inverts the anchor ranking. The model that raises the price collects the least of the rent, as the price-leadership model predicts.
why: Interesting LLM pricing-collusion simulation, but no real market data.

title: An Information-Theoretic and Metrics-driven Framework for Deep Hedging: From Path Generation to Production Observability
abstract: Deep Hedging has been instrumental in sparking dedicated research into utilizing Neural Networks (NNs) to solve financial hedging and pricing problems that previously relied on closed-form analytical solutions. Traditional analytical frameworks rely on idealized assumptions regarding market mechanisms-particularly continuous trading, frictionless execution, and complete markets. Bridging the gap between these idealized models and real-world market frictions has been the foundational motivation behind Deep Hedging research. This paper formulates Deep Hedging as a metrics-driven, closed-loop information system spanning from initial path generation through production observability. We introduce methods for synthesizing training trajectories with controlled statistical characteristics alongside an information-theoretic measurement framework to evaluate both data richness and model efficacy across specific market regimes. Ultimately, this end-to-end approach equips trading desks with fine-grained control over the statistical distributions governing model training and provides a rigorous, experimental telemetry framework for deploying and iteratively refining Deep Hedging systems.
why: Deep hedging observability framework; generic, unclear empirical evidence.

title: Asking for the Right Signal: Information Design and Portfolio Choice
abstract: Investors choose not only how much information to acquire, but also how predictive information is represented for decisions. This paper studies how signal form affects portfolio value. In a mean-variance problem, we consider binary tail-event, ternary range, and continuous level signals, with tail and range boundaries determined endogenously. Optimal signal boundaries may shift away from the prior mean toward more extreme return regions, revealing an exploratory feature of information design that generates more valuable posterior portfolio opportunities. Using LLM-based information extraction in commodity futures markets, we show through alternative prompts that the value of information depends not only on predictive content, but also on how it is represented for subsequent decisions.
why: Signal form in mean-variance with LLM extraction; theory-heavy, modest empirics.

title: Stress Testing and Explainable AI Frameworks for Deep Learning and Agentic Models in Credit Underwriting and Solvency Forecasting
abstract: This research proposes an explainable artificial intelligence system for assessing loan creditworthiness of borrowers, forecasting the solvency of institutions, conducting macroeconomic stress testing, and automatic risk reporting. LendingClub loan data have been combined with macroeconomic variables from FRED, whereas FDIC financial data have been used for institution-level analysis. Dif erent algorithms such as logistic regression, random forest, LightGBM, XGBoost, and deep neural network were assessed using chronological training, validation, and testing samples. XGBoost demonstrated the best results in terms of performance on a borrower level with 0.7197 and 0.7139 ROC-AUC scores on the validation and testing samples, correspondingly. The deep neural network generated similar discriminatory power but had lower specificity and more false positives. Multi-task LSTM was implemented to forecast the equity-to-assets ratio four quarters ahead and performed better than the benchmark model.The techniques SHAP and LIME recognized interest rate, FICO score, level of indebtedness, loan term, homeownership, and macroeconomic environment as key determinants that af ect credit risk prediction. Stress testing of the macroeconomic environment determined which borrowers are sensitive to negative scenarios, and the agentic reporting layer created structured reports for borrowers, explanations, stress test results, and human review flags. In general, the results show that the combination of predictive modelling, explainability, stress testing, and human review is possible.
why: Generic explainable credit and solvency pipeline; AI is framing.

title: Whom Should the Advisor Meet? Targeting Scarce Human Elicitation in AI-Enabled Financial
abstract: AI-enabled advisory services raise an operating question about how human and automated work should be divided. Automated systems can handle customers at low marginal cost, whereas human advisors are more expensive and constrained by available time. A human can nevertheless add value when the customer information needed for the recommendation is difficult to obtain automatically. We examine this trade-off when the human advantage is concentrated in preference elicitation rather than in portfolio optimization. We represent the advisory encounter as two connected stages. The first stage obtains information about a customer's private preference; the second uses that information to generate a recommendation. A customer-level measure, the net marginal value of human elicitation, links three decisions: whether to involve a human, which customers should receive human service when capacity is limited, and how much advisory capacity to provide. The measure reflects the improvement in information, the responsiveness of the downstream decision, the economic consequences of decision error, and the cost of human service. Using 19,022 respondents from the 2024 National Financial Capability Study, we estimate heterogeneous priors for investment risk tolerance and use them in the service-system model. The information and cost parameters that cannot be identified from the survey are calibrated. Under the baseline calibration, human-assisted elicitation is preferred for 37.65% of customers when capacity is unconstrained. With capacity fixed at 20% of the sample, the value-index policy produces $141,093 in aggregate net welfare relative to AI-only service, compared with $128,283 for wealth-based routing, $88,227 for complexity-based routing, and-$36,063 for uncertainty-based routing. The comparison indicates that the value of human involvement depends on how information changes the downstream decision, rather than on uncertainty or another customer characteristic taken by itself.
why: Advisory human-versus-automation targeting; conceptual model, limited implementation path.

title: The Effect of AI Agents on Switching Costs How Another Moat in Banking Is Being Filled
abstract: Retail banking relationships have historically been protected less by price than by the effort required to switch, researching alternatives, opening accounts, moving direct deposits, closing the old relationship. This effort based protection is referred to as a "switching cost moat." This paper investigates how agentic artificial intelligence, exemplified by Meta's Muse, launched September 8, 2026, which can compare deposit rates and execute financial transactions through a Plaid integration spanning over 12,000 institutions, may fill that moat by driving the effort cost of switching toward zero, independent of any change in the underlying rate incentive itself. This paper constructed the first rigorous, regulatory data grounded empirical baseline of how much this effort cost has historically suppressed rate driven deposit switching, using Federal Financial Institutions Examination Council (FFIEC) data for a selected bank sample (2006-2026) and National Credit Union Administration (NCUA) data for credit unions (2006-2021). This research found a real, statistically significant, but modest and continuous (not threshold) relationship, roughly 0.40 to 0.66 percentage points of deposit share migration per percentage point of rate spread, explaining at most 19-70% of quarterly variation depending on sample and sub-period. This baseline is situated against the 2013 launch of Yu'e Bao in China, in which one-click switching from payment app balances into a money market fund produced the fastest mutual fund growth ever recorded, and against mortgage lending, where borrowers already demonstrably pay a premium for reduced friction. Together, this evidence suggests the historical weakness of rate driven switching has been substantially an effort cost phenomenon, not a price awareness one, and that agentic AI, by construction, targets exactly that effort cost.
why: Agentic AI switching-cost banking study; speculative framing, thin data detail.

title: Long Text to Predictive Features: LLM-Guided Blockwise Feature Engineering via Executable Program Search
abstract: Industrial risk-control systems typically rely on structured-data models for efficient prediction, yet substantial valuable information remains embedded in unstructured long text. Extracting this information through manual feature engineering is labor-intensive, while requiring a large language model (LLM) to process every real-time input may not meet practical deployment requirements. To address this challenge, we propose LLM-BlockFE, an LLM-guided offline feature construction framework that converts long text into executable feature programs, thereby avoiding LLM calls during online inference. LLM-BlockFE constructs feature programs by incrementally appending immutable code blocks and evaluates candidate features using a downstream model. To address the tendency of conventional greedy search to become trapped in suboptimal solutions, our method introduces a block-level rollback mechanism based on depth-calibrated credit allocation and advances multiple independent search trajectories in an interleaved manner, reducing redundant exploration by sharing fixed descriptions of each trajectory's exploration direction. After the search, the resulting programs are frozen and deployed to extract structured features for downstream prediction models. Across two public and two private datasets, LLM-BlockFE achieves absolute AUC improvements of 0.0069 to 0.0358 over the strongest baseline on each dataset in the full-dataset comparison. Post-launch monitoring across five deployed financial risk-control applications shows absolute KS improvements of 0.02 to 1.56 percentage points over the existing manually designed strategy.
why: LLM-generated features for risk control; general text, finance link weak.

title: Artificial Intelligence Capital and Complementary Acquisitions *
abstract: This paper studies whether firms' accumulation of artificial intelligence (AI) capital shapes their participation in the market for corporate control. We combine AI-skilled employment data with a capitalization model to estimate the implied price and accumulated quantity of installed AI capital. A one-standard-deviation increase in AI capital is associated with a 2.21-percentage-point increase in the acquisition probability. The relation remains after controlling for AI-skilled employment, data-skilled hiring, organizational capital, and patent capital, whereas AI-skilled employment alone does not exhibit the same predictive relation. Cross-sectionally, the AI--acquisition relation is stronger among large firms. AI capital also predicts firms' subsequent demand for AI-skilled labor beyond existing AI employment and prior AI hiring activity. Consistent with complementarity between installed AI capabilities and additional AI expertise, AI-rich acquirers disproportionately select targets that employ AI-skilled workers, both in realized public-to-public deals and relative to matched potential targets. We further find that the positive relation between AI capital and acquisition activity is weaker when firms face higher financing costs, consistent with financing conditions affecting firms' ability to act on acquisition opportunities. The main relation is also present in instrumental-variable estimates using firms' pre-2010 exposure to AI-intensive universities. Together, the findings show that accumulated AI capabilities are associated with both greater acquisitiveness and the acquisition of complementary AI human capital, with implications for firm boundaries and the persistence of incumbent advantage.
why: Corporate finance AI-capital regression; AI is framing, not method.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Finance: From Prediction to Economic Value
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) expands financial prediction and information processing, but technical gains do not necessarily improve allocation. This theory-guided survey synthesizes 209 publications through information economics, constrained choice, delegation, and strategic feedback. We trace tool evolution and distinguish measurement, historical policy evaluation, observed adoption, and equilibrium mechanisms. Three conclusions organize the evidence. First, prediction gains create net value only through feasible actions after implementation costs. Second, more precise signals can improve selection while either expanding or contracting funding; contracts and capacity determine the allocation response. Third, human discretion and counterparty adaptation make deployed performance endogenous. A Gaussian benchmark and five conditional propositions explain these distinctions without claiming a new unified equilibrium. The literature supports task-specific information gains, heterogeneous credit-pricing counterfactuals, and issuer adaptation, while sustained deployment value, competitive rent erosion, and aggregate welfare remain less securely established. The synthesis identifies the assumptions behind apparently conflicting findings and prioritizes empirical designs that observe thresholds, rival access, recommendations, and executed decisions.
why: Survey of 209 publications; explicitly rejected article type.

title: Financial Statement Analysis and Profitability Forecasting using Machine Learning Models
abstract: Financial statement analysis plays a critical role in evaluating a firm's financial performance and supporting decision making processes. However, traditional analytical methods often struggle to capture complex and non-linear relationships present in financial data, limiting their predictive capability. This study proposes an integrated framework that combines financial statement analysis with machine learning techniques to improve the accuracy of profitability forecasting. The research utilizes structured financial data derived from income statements and balance sheets, which are transformed into meaningful financial ratios through feature engineering. Several machine learning models, including Decision Tree, Random Forest, K-Nearest Neighbors, and Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), are implemented and evaluated using standard performance metrics such as accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score. The results indicate that ensemble learning methods, particularly XGBoost, outperform other models in predicting firm profitability. The findings demonstrate that machine learning significantly enhances the effectiveness of financial analysis by capturing hidden patterns in financial data. This study contributes to the growing body of research on data-driven financial forecasting and provides a practical framework for investors, analysts, and financial institutions to improve decision-making processes.
why: Standard ML on financial ratios; no costs or novel evaluation.

title: Multi-period Mean-Expectile Portfolio Optimization under Wasserstein Ambiguity: Reformulation, Degeneracy and the Role of the Ground Metric
abstract: Expectiles are the only law-invariant risk measures that are both coherent and elicitable. Unlike Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR), however, they do not admit a Rockafellar--Uryasev representation that admits tractable Wasserstein reformulations. We address this difficulty by developing an envelope theorem for worst-case expectiles that characterizes the worst-case expectile over a Wasserstein ambiguity set as the unique root of a worst-case expectation with a two-piece affine integrand. This representation permits direct application of standard Wasserstein duality. Using this result, we reformulate a multi-period tri-level mean--expectile portfolio problem as four parametric linear programs with constraints. We establish four structural properties of the proposed model: an endogenously damped price of robustness, a decision-dependent critical radius beyond which the expectile tail component becomes inactive, exact recovery of the nominal model at zero ambiguity, and a characterization of how the Wasserstein ground metric determines whether the limiting portfolio becomes more concentrated or more diversified. Numerical experiments on 90 FTSE constituents over 3,341 out-of-sample trading days show that the expectile model outperforms a CVaR model matched on ambiguity set, radius, ground metric, and trade-off weight in all nine parameter cells---significantly so whenever the radius is non-trivial. The experiments further confirm the predicted degeneracy under the ground metric.
why: Wasserstein mean-expectile optimization; theory with no empirical path.

title: Large-Scale Benchmarking of Quantum Neural Network Configurations for Financial Time Series Forecasting
abstract: Quantum machine learning, and quantum neural networks (QNNs) in particular, are advancing fields with growing potential. Although systematic comparisons of QNN configurations have been explored primarily for classification tasks, comparatively little attention has been given to regression problems, particularly financial time series forecasting. This study presents a large-scale systematic comparative evaluation of QNN component configurations for financial time series forecasting, using the GBP/USD spot exchange rate as a case study. A grid search across encoding methods, ansatz designs, qubit counts, layer depths, and cost functions yields 1,368 distinct model configurations, each evaluated in terms of prediction accuracy, computational cost, and convergence behaviour. The results reveal unique insights into how the choice of methods influences performance, such as that gate selection and arrangement are more critical to model success than raw parameter count, and that entanglement is a system-level property of the full circuit rather than solely at the ansatz level. The best-performing QNN configuration achieves an $R^2$ score of 0.985, outperforming a classical BiLSTM baseline. Additionally, the impact of real quantum hardware noise is assessed through execution on the IQM Emerald device, revealing that gate errors and decoherence represent a significant barrier to practical deployment, with gate selection and circuit depth identified as key determinants of hardware noise resilience. Overall, the findings provide practical architectural guidance for QNN design and establish a baseline characterisation of QNN noise sensitivity on near-term quantum devices.
why: Quantum NN grid on GBP/USD forecasting; no costs or baseline discipline.

title: Data-Driven Approach to Forecasting Inflation in Bangladesh
abstract: The economy of Bangladesh has been on the rise over the past decade. One of the biggest factors contributing to the country's economic condition is the inflation rate. The increase in prices over a certain period is referred to as inflation. The project aimed to present a comprehensive analysis of forecasting the inflation rates in Bangladesh using Machine learning algorithms. The inflation rates are predicted using data over the last ten years. The data has been obtained from the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics. This study predicts inflation rates based on the following factors: CPI Value, Currency against USD, Money Supply, Interest Rates, GDP (in BDT), and GDP Per Capita and compares the performance of numerous models, finding that XGBoost is the most efficient algorithm, with Mean Absolute Error (MAE) of 0.193 and Mean Squared Error (MSE) of 0.062. Similarly, the Random forest model also performed better with low evaluation metrics. The findings indicate the exciting prospects of machine learning approaches for economic forecasting, particularly in emerging nations like Bangladesh.
why: Bangladesh inflation regression comparison; no transferable method.

title: The Invisible Executive: Decision Authority and Accountable AI in Credit Union Commercial Lending
abstract: Artificial intelligence can redistribute practical decision authority inside a financial institution without changing its organizational chart. This conceptual article examines that possibility in U.S. credit union commercial lending. It integrates selected research on automation, organizational control, human-AI collaboration, learning, and accountability with official lending and governance sources. The term invisible executive describes consequential influence embedded in workflows, rather than legal authority or software intent. The central argument is that accountable adoption requires institutions to preserve the knowledge, workable discretion, and resources needed to evaluate and challenge automated recommendations. Fictional scenarios illustrate how defaults, incentives, and review capacity could affect meaningful human involvement. A proposed decision authority review traces information preparation, analysis, recommendation, action, communication, and correction. The article examines human bias, vendor dependence, generative explanations, and the costs of additional scrutiny. It offers implementation recommendations and testable research propositions. The framework is an interpretive synthesis, not an empirically validated instrument. Its practical purpose is to help leaders assess whether their institutions can understand, evaluate, and correct consequential decisions throughout the lending relationship.
why: Conceptual credit union governance essay; no data or method.

title: Weighted selection from elliptical distributions: a stochastic representation and an application to portfolio separation
abstract: We represent (weighted-)selection-elliptical distributions as an affine combination of the $q$ selection variables plus an elliptical term whose direction alone is independent. This form suffices for $q+2$ fund separation via first-order stochastic dominance, inter alia relaxing Simaan's (1993) three-fund assumptions.
why: Elliptical distribution fund separation theorem; pure theory, no data.

title: Future Of Work: The Rising Dominance Of Ai Agentic Systems As A New Digital Workforce In The Future Job Market
abstract: The transition from generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) to agentic artificial intelligence (AI) changes the analytical problem of the future of work. Earlier automation research largely asked whether machines could perform particular tasks; current agentic systems add planning, tool use, memory, delegation, and multi-step execution, making it possible for a software system to occupy a more persistent position inside an organizational workflow. This systematic review synthesizes recent empirical, theoretical, and policy evidence on the emergence of AI agents as a prospective digital workforce and asks whether "AI as a workforce" is a meaningful analytical category rather than a rhetorical metaphor. Following PRISMAinformed procedures and a transparent multidisciplinary search protocol, the review integrates peerreviewed studies, working papers, large-scale labor-market datasets, and authoritative institutional reports published principally between 2018 and October 2026, with foundational work retained where theoretically indispensable. The synthesis identifies five recurring mechanisms: task substitution, task augmentation, coordination automation, new-task creation, and redistribution of human agency. Empirical evidence shows substantial productivity gains in bounded knowledge tasks, heterogeneous effects by worker skill and task type, and early evidence of task reorganization rather than immediate aggregate employment collapse. The World Economic Forum projects 170 million jobs created and 92 million displaced by 2030 across major macrotrends, while the International Labour Organization estimates that about one quarter of global employment is potentially exposed to GenAI, emphasizing that exposure is not a forecast of job loss. More recent agentic-AI scholarship suggests that autonomy itself becomes an organizational resource and risk. The review develops a novel "Agentic Workforce Transition" framework in which AI agents are treated as quasi-organizational actors whose economic effects depend on capability, autonomy, organizational embedding, and governance. The central critical proposition is an Agency Paradox: increasing machine autonomy may increase, rather than eliminate, the demand for human judgment, accountability, and system-level supervision-while simultaneously hollowing out the task-level experience through which expertise is traditionally acquired.
why: Systematic review on future of work; off-topic for finance.

title: From CARE to Compliance: Integrating Indigenous Data Governance into the NIST AI Risk Management Framework
abstract: The NIST AI Risk Management Framework (the “Framework” or “RMF”) has become a standard reference for AI risk management in the United States. Across the Framework, the AI RMF Playbook, the AI RMF Roadmap, the published crosswalks, and the Generative AI Profile, NIST’s materials nowhere mention Indigenous peoples, tribal governments, or tribal consultation, although AI training corpora already contain tribal languages and data about tribal lands and citizens. The Framework asks organizations to consult “affected communities” and to document “context-specific laws, norms and expectations,” but it never says which communities or whose laws. It deliberately leaves the specifics to adopters and, for particular settings or applications, to Profiles, and no Profile the author has found supplies them for the 575 federally recognized tribal nations. This Article supplies those specifics. The CARE Principles for Indigenous Data Governance (Collective Benefit, Authority to Control, Responsibility, and Ethics) set out how Indigenous data should be governed. The Article builds what is, to the author’s knowledge, the first connection between the two systems at the level of the numbered subcategory: a crosswalk that maps each CARE principle onto specific RMF subcategories. Three implementation Profiles put the crosswalk into practice: one for federal agencies whose AI touches tribal citizens, lands, or data; one for private developers whose corpora contain Indigenous data; and one for tribal governments building their own AI governance capacity. The third is a model Tribal Profile of the Framework; the author’s review through September 2026 found no other Profile designed for tribal adoption. The Article grounds tribal authority over data in inherent sovereignty, the powers of self-government that predate the Constitution and were never delegated by it, and not in research ethics, equity, the trust responsibility, or consultation. How far that authority reaches nonmember AI developers under the consensual-relationship and direct-effects exceptions of Montana v. United States is contested; the Article argues that it reaches them most securely by consent. Federal policy calls for equity language to be stripped from the Framework itself, and claims framed as equity would lose their basis in the Framework along with that language. A claim grounded in sovereignty does not depend on that language, because tribal sovereignty does not derive from federal policy. The Article draws on three documented cases of extraction: the Havasupai blood samples, the Lakota language recordings, and the te reo Māori recordings scraped from the web and used to train OpenAI’s Whisper. It asks who has authority to decide how Indigenous peoples’ data may be used, including to train AI systems.
why: Indigenous data governance in NIST framework; not finance.

title: AdaptLSTM: Efficient Adaptive Online Learning for Cloud Workload Forecasting under Distribution Drift
abstract: Accurate workload forecasting is critical for elastic resource provisioning in web-scale cloud services, where distribution shifts driven by viral content, product launches, and user behavior degrade offline-trained models rapidly. Naive online learning recovers accuracy but incurs prohibitive per-step compute cost. We propose AdaptLSTM, an adaptive online framework that detects drift via validation-calibrated thresholds and applies selective, targeted updates. On the Alibaba Machine Trace, AdaptLSTM recovers 54\% of Naive Online's improvement at 20\% cost ($2.7\times$ efficiency, $p=0.002$ over 10 seeds). On the more volatile Container Trace, it achieves 96\% at 20\% cost ($4.8\times$ efficiency, $+75\%$ MAE reduction over Static). Unlike classical drift detectors (ADWIN, DDM, Page-Hinkley) which fail to trigger on regression-scale error streams, AdaptLSTM fires 42 times over 301 steps and outperforms matched-budget baselines. Wall-clock profiling shows $1.33\times$ throughput gain and 45\% update-time reduction. The framework is model-agnostic: identical Pareto patterns hold for LSTM, GRU, and Transformer backbones.
why: Cloud workload forecasting; off-topic.
